title: Scaling Laws & Lost-in-the-Middle
scopeHtml: Scope: The relationship between model size, data and compute, and why models miss information in long contexts.

notes.title: Power laws from zero
notes.html:
A scaling law is a measured rule that says: if you make a model bigger, give it more training text, or spend more compute, its error (the loss) goes down in a predictable way. Predictable is the key word. Before scaling laws, training a giant model was a gamble. After them, a lab can train ten small models, draw a line through the results, and forecast how a model 1,000 times bigger will behave before paying for it.

Some vocabulary first, because everything below uses it.

  • Parameter: one learned number (a weight) inside the model. "7B" means about 7 billion of them. Written N.
  • Token: a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of an English word. Training data is counted in tokens. Written D (data).
  • FLOP: one floating-point operation (one multiply or add). Total training work is the compute C. A training run for a frontier model is on the order of 10^24 to 10^26 FLOPs (verify for the newest models; labs rarely publish exact numbers).
  • Loss: how surprised the model is by the correct next token, averaged over a held-out text set. Lower is better. It is measured in nats (natural log units) per token. Perplexity is e^loss.
  • Power law: a relationship of the form y = a * x^(-b). Double x and y shrinks by a fixed factor, not a fixed amount.

Why a power law and not a straight line? Because each extra bit of quality is harder than the last. Think of the loss as a distance to a floor (the irreducible randomness of language). Early on, a bigger model fixes lots of easy mistakes. Later it fixes rarer, subtler ones. The gain per doubling shrinks, but the shrinkage is so regular that on a log-log plot (both axes logarithmic) the curve becomes a straight line:

log(loss - floor)
   |\
   | \
   |  \          slope = -alpha  (small, e.g. -0.3)
   |   \
   |    \_____
   +----------------- log(parameters N)

A tiny worked example. Suppose loss - floor = 400 / N^0.34. Going from N = 1e9 to N = 2e9 multiplies the excess loss by 2^-0.34 = 0.79. So each doubling of the model removes about 21 percent of the remaining excess loss. Ten doublings (a 1,024 times bigger model) multiply it by 0.79^10 = 0.095, so about 90 percent of the excess is gone. The exponents are small, which is why you need orders of magnitude more resources for each visible step.

Real users of this idea: OpenAI's GPT-4 technical report said it predicted the final loss of the large run from runs using 1,000 to 10,000 times less compute. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper, Meta's Llama papers and the Pythia and OLMo open suites all fit scaling curves the same way. Every serious pretraining team runs a "scaling ladder" of small models before the big run.

Everyday analogy: the speed of a marathon runner versus years of training. The first year of training takes you from 5 hours to 4. The tenth year shaves seconds. The improvement is regular and plottable, but each step costs far more than the one before.

See also in 06_S1: the short Kaplan versus Chinchilla summary and the 6ND rule. This note goes deeper into the formula, the numbers, the code, and then spends half its length on lost-in-the-middle.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "loss falls linearly with size". It falls as a power law; each doubling gives a smaller absolute gain.
  • Confusing loss with benchmark accuracy. Scaling laws are cleanest for loss; task scores can jump or plateau (see 06_S1, emergence).
  • Forgetting the floor. Loss never reaches zero because text has real randomness; the formula has an irreducible term.
  • Assuming a law fitted on small models is a guarantee. It is a forecast with error bars.

notes.title: The Chinchilla loss formula with real numbers
notes.html:
Hoffmann et al. (2022, DeepMind) fitted a single equation to hundreds of training runs:

L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta

Read it as three separate costs added together:

  • E: the irreducible loss, the entropy of language itself. No model can beat it.
  • A / N^alpha: the penalty for the model being too small. It shrinks as parameters grow.
  • B / D^beta: the penalty for too little data. It shrinks as tokens grow.

The published fit (their "approach 3") reports roughly E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, alpha = 0.34, beta = 0.28. Treat these as illustrative and verify against the paper before quoting them; later replications found they shift with the tokenizer, data mix and architecture. What matters is the structure: two independent penalties, one for model size and one for data.

Let us compute by hand, showing the math, for two famous models.

Chinchilla: N = 70e9, D = 1.4e12.

  • N^0.34: ln(70e9) = 24.972, times 0.34 = 8.490, e^8.490 = 4,868. So A/N^alpha = 406.4 / 4868 = 0.0835.
  • D^0.28: ln(1.4e12) = 27.968, times 0.28 = 7.831, e^7.831 = 2,517. So B/D^beta = 410.7 / 2517 = 0.1632.
  • L = 1.69 + 0.0835 + 0.1632 = 1.937.

Gopher: N = 280e9, D = 300e9.

  • ln(280e9) = 26.358, times 0.34 = 8.962, e^8.962 = 7,801, A/N^alpha = 0.0521.
  • ln(300e9) = 26.427, times 0.28 = 7.400, e^7.400 = 1,635, B/D^beta = 0.2512.
  • L = 1.69 + 0.0521 + 0.2512 = 1.993.

Gopher has four times the parameters, so its model penalty is smaller (0.052 versus 0.084). But it saw 4.7 times fewer tokens, so its data penalty is much larger (0.251 versus 0.163). Net: Chinchilla is lower by about 0.056 nats with the same compute. That one calculation is the whole Chinchilla story: Gopher was starved of data.

Code: predict loss from N and D.

# Predict pretraining loss with the Chinchilla-style formula (constants: verify against the paper)
E, A, B, ALPHA, BETA = 1.69, 406.4, 410.7, 0.34, 0.28

def loss(n_params: float, n_tokens: float) -> float:
    return E + A / n_params**ALPHA + B / n_tokens**BETA

print(round(loss(70e9, 1.4e12), 3))   # ~1.937 (Chinchilla)
print(round(loss(280e9, 300e9), 3))   # ~1.993 (Gopher)
import kotlin.math.pow

// Same formula; prints ~1.937 and ~1.993
const val E = 1.69
const val A = 406.4
const val B = 410.7
const val ALPHA = 0.34
const val BETA = 0.28

fun loss(nParams: Double, nTokens: Double): Double =
    E + A / nParams.pow(ALPHA) + B / nTokens.pow(BETA)

fun main() {
    println("%.3f".format(loss(70e9, 1.4e12)))
    println("%.3f".format(loss(280e9, 300e9)))
}
// Same formula; prints ~1.937 and ~1.993
public class ChinchillaLoss {
    static final double E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, ALPHA = 0.34, BETA = 0.28;

    static double loss(double nParams, double nTokens) {
        return E + A / Math.pow(nParams, ALPHA) + B / Math.pow(nTokens, BETA);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%.3f%n", loss(70e9, 1.4e12));
        System.out.printf("%.3f%n", loss(280e9, 300e9));
    }
}

Everyday analogy: a restaurant's quality depends on the chef's skill (model size) and on the quality and amount of ingredients (data). A superstar chef with a nearly empty pantry loses to a good chef with a full one. The formula is the accounting of both shortfalls.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting the constants as exact truths. They are fitted values for one setup; say "roughly" and "verify".
  • Forgetting E. Without the floor term the formula would predict perfect models at infinite size.
  • Treating alpha and beta as equal. They are close (0.34 and 0.28), which is why the optimum scales both roughly together.
  • Explaining Chinchilla as "bigger is better". It is "balanced is better for a fixed compute budget".

notes.title: Compute-optimal allocation step by step
notes.html:
The practical question is: I have a fixed compute budget C. How big should the model be, and how many tokens should I train on? Two facts make this solvable.

  1. Compute accounting. For a dense transformer, training costs about C = 6 * N * D FLOPs. Where does 6 come from? The forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (one multiply, one add). The backward pass costs about twice the forward (gradients with respect to activations and weights), so 4. Total 2 + 4 = 6. This ignores attention over very long sequences and is approximate.
  2. The loss formula above. Minimising L subject to 6ND = C gives a pair (N, D).

The result (their three methods agree within error): both N_opt and D_opt grow as roughly the square root of compute, and the ratio comes out near 20 tokens per parameter. Using D = 20N: C = 6 * N * 20N = 120 N^2, so N = sqrt(C / 120).

Step 1: pick a budget            C = 5.76e23 FLOPs
Step 2: N = sqrt(C / 120)        sqrt(4.8e21) = 6.93e10   (about 70B)
Step 3: D = 20 * N               1.39e12                  (about 1.4T tokens)
Step 4: check C = 6 * N * D      6 * 6.93e10 * 1.39e12 = 5.78e23  OK

That budget was chosen to reproduce Chinchilla; the answer lands almost exactly on 70B parameters and 1.4T tokens. Another check: a 7B model needs 20 * 7e9 = 140e9 tokens and 6 * 7e9 * 140e9 = 5.9e21 FLOPs. On a GPU delivering, say, 4e14 useful FLOP/s (a plausible sustained figure for a modern accelerator at about 40 percent utilisation; verify for your hardware), that is 5.9e21 / 4e14 = 1.5e7 GPU-seconds, about 1.5e7 / 3600 = 4,100 GPU-hours. With 512 GPUs it is about 8 hours. Math shown, so you can redo it for any size.

import math

def compute_optimal(flops: float, tokens_per_param: float = 20.0):
    # C = 6*N*D and D = k*N  =>  N = sqrt(C / (6*k))
    n = math.sqrt(flops / (6 * tokens_per_param))
    return n, tokens_per_param * n

n, d = compute_optimal(5.76e23)
print(f"{n:.3g} params, {d:.3g} tokens")   # ~6.93e+10 params, ~1.39e+12 tokens
import kotlin.math.sqrt

fun computeOptimal(flops: Double, tokensPerParam: Double = 20.0): Pair<Double, Double> {
    val n = sqrt(flops / (6 * tokensPerParam))
    return n to tokensPerParam * n
}

fun main() {
    val (n, d) = computeOptimal(5.76e23)
    println("%.3g params, %.3g tokens".format(n, d)) // ~6.93e+10, ~1.39e+12
}
public class ComputeOptimal {
    static double[] computeOptimal(double flops, double tokensPerParam) {
        double n = Math.sqrt(flops / (6 * tokensPerParam));
        return new double[] { n, tokensPerParam * n };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] nd = computeOptimal(5.76e23, 20.0);
        System.out.printf("%.3g params, %.3g tokens%n", nd[0], nd[1]); // ~6.93e+10, ~1.39e+12
    }
}

Real products: the Chinchilla ratio shaped the planning of LLaMA 1 (65B on 1.4T tokens, intentionally near the rule) and many 2022-2023 models. Training teams use this calculator on day one of a project to size the cluster rental.

Everyday analogy: you have a fixed monthly food budget. Spending it all on a fancy oven (model) leaves nothing for groceries (data), and the reverse leaves you with a pile of food and a camping stove. The optimum splits it so the last pound spent on either gives the same improvement.

Common interview traps.

  • Giving C = 6ND without being able to justify the 6 (2 forward plus 4 backward).
  • Applying 6ND to mixture-of-experts models using total parameters. For MoE use active parameters per token (see 04_T2).
  • Saying "20 tokens per parameter is a law of nature". It is a fit that moves with data quality and architecture.
  • Mixing up FLOPs (a count) with FLOP/s (a rate) when converting to GPU-hours.

notes.title: Overtraining and inference-aware scaling
notes.html:
Chinchilla answers: "cheapest way to reach a given loss, counting only the training bill." But a deployed model is called billions of times. Each generated token costs about 2N FLOPs of inference (just the forward pass). Lifetime cost is:

total = 6*N*D  (training, paid once)  +  2*N*T  (serving, T = tokens served over the lifetime)

If T is large, a smaller N trained on a larger D wins. This is called overtraining (or "inference-aware" training; see Sardana and Frankle, 2023, "Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal", verify citation details).

Worked example using the formula above. Meta trained Llama 3 8B on about 15T tokens (published figure; verify).

  • Training compute: 6 * 8e9 * 15e12 = 7.2e23 FLOPs.
  • Loss (formula): N^0.34 term = 406.4/2328 = 0.1746; D^0.28 term = 410.7/4889 = 0.0840; L = 1.69 + 0.1746 + 0.0840 = 1.949.
  • The Chinchilla-optimal model for the same 7.2e23 FLOPs: N = sqrt(7.2e23/120) = 7.75e10 (77B) on 1.55e12 tokens, with L = 1.929.

So the 77B model is better by only 0.02 nats at equal training compute, yet it costs 77/8 = 9.6 times more FLOPs on every generated token. If you serve trillions of tokens, the 8B wins on total cost. This is exactly why the ratio of tokens to parameters for 2023-2025 open models is hundreds, not 20: 15e12 / 8e9 = 1,875.

Chinchilla optimal    : 77B on 1.5T tokens  -> L ~ 1.929, serving ~9.6x costlier
Overtrained (Llama 3) :  8B on  15T tokens  -> L ~ 1.949, cheap to serve

There is a limit. Returns on extra tokens still follow B / D^beta, so overtraining has diminishing returns, and eventually you run out of unique high-quality text (the data wall, see 06_S1). Repeating data more than a few epochs gives progressively less value.

Another real-world force: the model also gets distilled or quantised later, and smaller models fit on phones. Gemini Nano and the on-device models Android ships are tiny because inference memory and battery, not training cost, are the binding constraint.

Code: lifetime cost comparison.

def lifetime_flops(n_params, train_tokens, served_tokens):
    return 6 * n_params * train_tokens + 2 * n_params * served_tokens

served = 2e13  # 20T tokens served over the model's life (assumption)
big = lifetime_flops(77e9, 1.55e12, served)   # Chinchilla-optimal
small = lifetime_flops(8e9, 15e12, served)    # overtrained
print(f"{big:.2e} vs {small:.2e}")            # 3.80e+24 vs 1.04e+24 -> small is ~3.6x cheaper overall
fun lifetimeFlops(n: Double, trainTokens: Double, servedTokens: Double) =
    6 * n * trainTokens + 2 * n * servedTokens

fun main() {
    val served = 2e13
    println("%.2e".format(lifetimeFlops(77e9, 1.55e12, served))) // 3.80e+24
    println("%.2e".format(lifetimeFlops(8e9, 15e12, served)))   // 1.04e+24
}
public class Lifetime {
    static double lifetimeFlops(double n, double trainTokens, double servedTokens) {
        return 6 * n * trainTokens + 2 * n * servedTokens;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double served = 2e13;
        System.out.printf("%.2e%n", lifetimeFlops(77e9, 1.55e12, served)); // 3.80e+24
        System.out.printf("%.2e%n", lifetimeFlops(8e9, 15e12, served));   // 1.04e+24
    }
}

Check by hand: big = 6*77e9*1.55e12 = 7.16e23 plus 2*77e9*2e13 = 3.08e24, total 3.80e24. Small = 6*8e9*15e12 = 7.2e23 plus 2*8e9*2e13 = 3.2e23, total 1.04e24. The small model is about 3.6 times cheaper overall under this assumed serving volume.

Everyday analogy: buying a car. A cheaper-to-build engine that guzzles fuel looks good on the sticker but loses over 200,000 km. Overtraining pays more upfront to get an engine that is cheap to run.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Chinchilla is "wrong". It optimises training cost; deployment changes the objective.
  • Forgetting to include serving volume. Without T you cannot choose between the two models.
  • Claiming unlimited gains from more tokens. The D^-beta term flattens and the data wall bites.
  • Using inference cost 6N per token; serving is a forward pass only, about 2N (plus attention and KV cache overhead).

notes.title: Fitting a scaling law yourself
notes.html:
You do not need a cluster to practise. The method labs use:

  1. Train 5 to 10 small models at different sizes (and data amounts), each properly tuned (learning rate matters a lot; a badly tuned run breaks the line).
  2. Record the final held-out loss of each.
  3. Subtract an estimated floor E and fit a straight line on log-log axes: log(L - E) = log(a) - b * log(N).
  4. Extrapolate to the target size and compare against a held-back mid-sized run to check the fit before trusting it.
import numpy as np

# Pretend measurements: (params, loss). Floor E is assumed known.
N = np.array([1e7, 3e7, 1e8, 3e8, 1e9])
L = np.array([3.62, 3.28, 2.95, 2.70, 2.48])
E = 1.69

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(N), np.log(L - E), 1)   # slope = -alpha
alpha, a = -slope, np.exp(intercept)
pred = lambda n: E + a / n**alpha
print(f"alpha={alpha:.2f}, predicted loss at 1e10: {pred(1e10):.2f}")

This part is training-side analysis, normally done in Python with numpy or SciPy curve_fit; Kotlin and Java have no sensible equivalent for a quick log-log regression (you would hand-code least squares, which adds nothing to the idea), so there is no snippet for them.

What can go wrong when you fit:

  • Wrong floor. If E is off, the log-log line bends and your exponent is wrong. Fit E jointly with a nonlinear least-squares method, and report error bars.
  • Too narrow a range. Models within a factor of 10 give a noisy slope. Use at least 2 to 3 orders of magnitude.
  • Untuned small runs. Optimal learning rate and batch size change with size. Tune per size or use a transfer method such as muP (verify).
  • Moving data mix. If the data changes between runs, the lines are not comparable.

Real users: the GPT-4 report's "predictable scaling" section, EleutherAI Pythia (a controlled ladder from 70M to 12B for studying exactly this), and the Llama 3 paper, which fitted scaling laws to pick the model size for its flagship run (verify exact details).

Everyday analogy: a carpenter tests joints in small offcuts before committing the expensive oak. The offcuts must be cut with the same care, or they tell you nothing about the real table.

Common interview traps.

  • Fitting a line to raw loss rather than loss minus the floor.
  • Reporting an extrapolation with no uncertainty.
  • Comparing runs at equal training steps instead of equal tokens.
  • Ignoring that one bad run (loss spike, wrong learning rate) can distort the whole fit.

notes.title: What scaling laws miss and how teams use them
notes.html:
Scaling laws are widely used, and widely misread. Here is a calibrated view.

What they are good for:

  • Budgeting: choose model size and token count before renting the cluster.
  • Forecasting: predict the loss of the final run, so a surprise deviation signals a bug (data corruption, numerical instability).
  • Ablations: compare architectures or data mixes by whether their curve sits lower, not by single numbers.
  • Product planning: if you buy API access, price drops and quality gains track these curves, so plan for next year's small model to beat this year's big one.

What they miss:

  • Task performance. Loss is an average over all tokens. A user cares about code correctness or tool use, which can lag or lead the loss (see emergence in 06_S1).
  • Data quality. Filtered, deduplicated, higher-quality data shifts the curve down; the same D is not the same value. Textbook-style synthetic data (the Phi models) showed small models gaining a lot from data quality (verify specifics).
  • Post-training. Instruction tuning, preference optimisation and reasoning training (see 05_R1) add capability not captured by pretraining loss.
  • Architecture changes. Mixture of experts, state-space layers and new attention schemes change the constants.
  • Test-time compute. Reasoning models spend compute per query, which is a separate scaling axis (see 06_S1 and 04_T2).
  • Regime changes. Multi-epoch training, synthetic data fractions and multimodal data are outside the original fits.

Production failure patterns from teams misusing the laws:

  • Choosing a model by the headline parameter count when two models differ in tokens trained and data quality (an older 70B can lose to a newer 8B).
  • Assuming a fine-tuned small model will keep following the pretraining curve (fine-tuning has its own, much flatter, scaling).
  • Over-promising to stakeholders: "next year's 10x compute gives 10x better", when the exponent says the loss drops by only a modest factor.

Everyday analogy: weather forecasts follow stable physics but break at the edge of what has been measured. A sensible planner uses them for the week ahead, not for a specific day six months away.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating loss and capability as the same thing.
  • Not mentioning data quality as a separate axis from data quantity.
  • Claiming scaling "has hit a wall" or "will continue forever" without separating pretraining, data supply and test-time compute. Present both sides and mark the debate as fast-moving (verify).
  • Assuming a law derived for dense transformers applies unchanged to MoE or hybrid models.

notes.title: Lost in the middle: what the experiment found
notes.html:
Now the second topic. A context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can read in one request (prompt plus answer). Windows have grown from 4,000 tokens to hundreds of thousands and beyond (verify current numbers per model). The natural hope: if the window is 200,000 tokens, the model uses all of it equally well. It does not.

Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., Stanford and collaborators, 2023; published in TACL 2024) ran a simple, clever test. Take a question with one document that holds the answer, mix it with 9, 19 or 29 distractor documents (retrieved passages that look relevant but do not contain the answer), and move the answer document to different positions. Measure accuracy at each position.

accuracy
  |*                                      *
  | *                                   *
  |   *                              *
  |      *  *  *  *  *  *  *  *  *
  +------------------------------------------
   first                              last
        position of the answer document

The curve is U shaped: best when the answer is first (the primacy effect) or last (the recency effect), worst in the middle. In the paper, for some models with 20 documents, accuracy with the answer in the middle fell below even the "closed-book" setting where the model got no documents at all. That is striking: extra context actively hurt (verify the exact figures in the paper; they differ per model and setting). The same U shape appeared in a second test, key-value retrieval: given a long JSON of random key-value pairs, return the value of one key. Even that trivial lookup degraded in the middle for several models. Models explicitly trained for long context were more robust but still showed some of the effect in the original study.

Why does it matter to a developer? Because RAG systems stuff retrieved chunks into prompts, chat apps stuff history, agents stuff tool results, and code assistants stuff files. In all of them, there is a "dead zone" in the middle where information is used unreliably.

Important nuance: newer models (2024 to 2026) have improved on simple single-fact retrieval, and vendors publish near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack charts (see 07_W1). But harder tasks (many facts to combine, similar-looking distractors, reasoning rather than copying) still show position and length effects in independent studies such as RULER and Chroma's "context rot" report (verify citations). Do not assume your model is immune; measure.

Everyday analogy: when someone reads you a long shopping list aloud, you remember the first few items and the last few, and the middle blurs. Writing the list down helps, but only if you actually look at it.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing it as "the model forgets the middle". The information is in the input; the model fails to use it reliably.
  • Saying it only affects old models. It is reduced but not gone, especially for multi-fact reasoning.
  • Claiming needle-in-a-haystack results disprove the effect. That test is easy (see 07_W1).
  • Quoting the original paper's numbers without noting that it tested 2023 models.

notes.title: Why models lose the middle
notes.html:
No single cause is proven; researchers have several well-supported contributors. Explaining them shows depth.

1. Causal masking creates a first-token advantage. In a decoder-only model each token can only attend to earlier tokens. So the first tokens are visible to every later token, while the last tokens are visible to few. The first token often becomes an attention sink: it soaks up a large share of attention weight regardless of content (Xiao et al., 2023, "Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks", the StreamingLLM paper). Early positions get disproportionate, stable treatment, which helps primacy.

2. Recency from training and positional encoding. Most training text depends heavily on nearby tokens (the next word is mostly predicted from the last few sentences). Positional schemes such as RoPE (rotary position embeddings, used by Llama, Qwen, Mistral and others) have a built-in tendency for attention scores to decay as distance grows. Distant tokens get less pull, so the end of the prompt (close to where generation happens) is strongly attended. Primacy plus recency gives the U.

3. Softmax dilution. Attention weights come from a softmax over all positions, so they sum to 1. If a relevant token gets a score advantage of delta over the typical token, its weight is:

weight = e^delta / (e^delta + (n - 1))

With delta = 5 (e^5 = 148):

  • n = 1,000 tokens: 148 / (148 + 999) = 0.129.
  • n = 100,000 tokens: 148 / (148 + 99,999) = 0.0015.

The same relevant token receives about 87 times less attention weight in the longer prompt, simply because there are more competitors. The model can compensate by sharpening scores (larger delta), but that must be learned, and learning it for every position at huge lengths is hard. This is the arithmetic behind "context rot".

4. Training data distribution. Long documents with important information buried deep are rare in training data, and long-context ability is often added late with limited long-text training (a "context extension" phase, see 07_W1). Models see fewer examples of needing a fact from position 60,000.

5. Distractors that look relevant. The attention can latch onto passages that resemble the question. The harder the distractors, the worse the failure, which is why hard-negative-rich retrieval output (typical in RAG) is a worst case.

Real mitigations seen in model development: continued training on long, synthetic retrieval-style tasks (position-balanced data), better length extrapolation methods (YaRN, position interpolation), and training objectives that reward using mid-context facts. Vendors report improved scores, but exact methods are mostly undisclosed (verify).

Everyday analogy: a teacher grading 200 essays remembers the first few, who set the standard, and the last few, because they are fresh. By essay 100 each one gets less attention because there is just more to hold.

Common interview traps.

  • Giving one cause as "the" cause. Several effects stack; say so.
  • Confusing attention sinks (a stable phenomenon on the first token) with "the model likes beginnings".
  • Forgetting that a retrieved-document list in a RAG prompt is the typical hard case with many look-alike distractors.
  • Believing a bigger window alone fixes it. Window size is capacity, not use.

notes.title: Measuring position sensitivity on your own data
notes.html:
Do not trust charts; build the test. The protocol is a position sweep:

  1. Take a set of 50 to 200 real questions with known answers and the passage that contains each answer (the "gold" passage).
  2. For each question, build prompts where the gold passage is at depth 0 percent (first), 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent (last), surrounded by distractor passages from your own corpus.
  3. Repeat at several total lengths (for example 4k, 16k, 64k tokens).
  4. Score each answer (exact match, or an LLM judge with a rubric) and plot accuracy by depth and length.

The result is a heat map: depth on one axis, length on the other. The region where accuracy drops below your quality bar is the effective context for your task. Set your production limit comfortably inside it.

import random
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"              # model id: verify in docs

def build_prompt(gold: str, distractors: list[str], depth: float, question: str) -> str:
    docs = distractors[:]
    docs.insert(round(depth * len(docs)), gold)       # depth 0.0 = first, 1.0 = last
    body = "\n\n".join(f"<doc id={i}>{d}</doc>" for i, d in enumerate(docs))
    return f"{body}\n\nAnswer using the documents only.\nQuestion: {question}"

def accuracy_at(depth, cases) -> float:
    hits = 0
    for gold, distractors, question, answer in cases:
        p = build_prompt(gold, random.sample(distractors, len(distractors)), depth, question)
        r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=100,
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": p}])
        hits += answer.lower() in r.content[0].text.lower()
    return hits / len(cases)

# for d in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0): print(d, accuracy_at(d, cases))  # prints one accuracy per depth
// Prompt builder for the position sweep; call your model client of choice with the result.
fun buildPrompt(gold: String, distractors: List<String>, depth: Double, question: String): String {
    val docs = distractors.toMutableList()
    docs.add(Math.round(depth * docs.size).toInt(), gold)   // 0.0 first ... 1.0 last
    val body = docs.mapIndexed { i, d -> "<doc id=$i>$d</doc>" }.joinToString("\n\n")
    return "$body\n\nAnswer using the documents only.\nQuestion: $question"
}

fun main() {
    val p = buildPrompt("Paris is the capital of France.", listOf("Cats purr.", "Rain falls."), 0.5,
        "What is the capital of France?")
    println(p) // gold document sits in the middle (id=1)
}
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class PositionSweep {
    static String buildPrompt(String gold, List<String> distractors, double depth, String question) {
        List<String> docs = new ArrayList<>(distractors);
        docs.add((int) Math.round(depth * docs.size()), gold);   // 0.0 first ... 1.0 last
        StringBuilder body = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < docs.size(); i++) {
            body.append("<doc id=").append(i).append(">").append(docs.get(i)).append("</doc>\n\n");
        }
        return body + "Answer using the documents only.\nQuestion: " + question;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(buildPrompt("Paris is the capital of France.",
            List.of("Cats purr.", "Rain falls."), 0.5, "What is the capital of France?"));
        // gold document sits in the middle (id=1)
    }
}

For Kotlin and Java, send the built prompt with the Anthropic Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java, AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(), then client.messages().create(...); verify exact builder names in the SDK docs) from a backend, never from an Android app holding the key.

Tips for a trustworthy sweep: shuffle distractors with a fixed seed, run at temperature 0, use enough questions (with 50 questions a 10 point difference is only barely above noise; compute a confidence interval), and keep the question wording identical across positions.

Everyday analogy: a doctor does not trust a drug because the leaflet says "works well"; they check it in their own patients. A position sweep is the clinical trial for your prompt.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing with synthetic filler instead of your real distractors; real retrieved chunks are much harder.
  • Not randomising distractor order, so position is confounded with content.
  • Reading a single run at one length and concluding "no problem".
  • Using an LLM judge without checking it against a few human-labelled answers.

notes.title: Prompt-level fixes: ordering, quoting and compression
notes.html:
Once you know the dead zone exists, you design around it. The cheapest fixes are in how the prompt is assembled.

1. Edge placement. Retrievers return chunks ranked by relevance, best first. If you paste them in rank order, rank 5 and rank 6 land in the middle. Reorder so the best chunks sit at the two edges and the weakest sit in the middle (LangChain calls its version LongContextReorder; verify the class name in current docs). Example for ranks 1 to 6:

retrieval order : 1 2 3 4 5 6   (1 = best)
edge placement  : 1 3 5 6 4 2   (best at the start and end, weakest in the middle)

2. Question last. Put long documents first and the instruction plus the question at the end, closest to where generation starts. Anthropic's long-context guidance advises documents first, query last (verify in current docs); it can improve quality noticeably on multi-document inputs.

3. Quote then answer. Ask the model to first copy the relevant quotes into a <quotes> section, then answer from them. The quoting step forces a retrieval operation over the whole context, and the answer step then works on a short, focused text sitting at the end of the context.

4. Fewer, better chunks. Cut top_k from 20 to 5 with a reranker (a cross-encoder that rescores query-chunk pairs, see 01_E1). Less context is often better than more.

5. Structure. Wrap each document in tags with an id and title so the model can refer to them, and so you can check citations automatically.

6. Compress or summarise. Replace bulky tool outputs and old conversation turns with summaries, and keep a "pinned" system section at the start.

7. Repeat the critical rule. For very long prompts, restate the essential instruction at the end. Costs a few tokens, helps recency.

Code: edge-placement reorder.

def edge_reorder(ranked: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """ranked[0] is the best chunk. Best go to both ends, worst to the middle."""
    front, back = [], []
    for i, chunk in enumerate(ranked):
        (front if i % 2 == 0 else back).append(chunk)
    return front + back[::-1]

print(edge_reorder(["r1", "r2", "r3", "r4", "r5", "r6"]))
# ['r1', 'r3', 'r5', 'r6', 'r4', 'r2']
fun <T> edgeReorder(ranked: List<T>): List<T> {
    val front = ranked.filterIndexed { i, _ -> i % 2 == 0 }
    val back = ranked.filterIndexed { i, _ -> i % 2 == 1 }
    return front + back.reversed()
}

fun main() {
    println(edgeReorder(listOf("r1", "r2", "r3", "r4", "r5", "r6")))
    // [r1, r3, r5, r6, r4, r2]
}
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public class EdgeReorder {
    static <T> List<T> edgeReorder(List<T> ranked) {
        List<T> front = new ArrayList<>(), back = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < ranked.size(); i++) {
            (i % 2 == 0 ? front : back).add(ranked.get(i));
        }
        Collections.reverse(back);
        front.addAll(back);
        return front;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(edgeReorder(List.of("r1", "r2", "r3", "r4", "r5", "r6")));
        // [r1, r3, r5, r6, r4, r2]
    }
}

Two more prompt snippets that go with the code. Quote-then-answer instruction:

First, find the quotes from the documents that are relevant to the question and
put them in <quotes> tags with the document id. If there are none, say so.
Then answer using only those quotes, citing document ids.

Everyday analogy: a speaker puts the most important points in the opening and the closing, because the audience's attention is highest there. Reordering chunks is applying that rhetoric to a model.

Common interview traps.

  • Reordering without a measure. Run the position sweep before and after; the gain depends on model and task.
  • Putting the question only at the start of a 100k-token prompt.
  • Stuffing 30 chunks "to be safe". More distractors hurt, and cost more per call.
  • Forgetting that edge placement and prompt caching conflict if the edges change per query: keep the stable material first (cacheable) and the variable material after it.

notes.title: Architecture-level answers and when to switch strategy
notes.html:
When prompt tweaks are not enough, change the system.

  • RAG with a reranker (see 07_W1 for the long context versus RAG table): only the top few chunks enter the prompt, so there is no middle.
  • Map-reduce or hierarchical summarisation: process each document separately (map), then combine short results (reduce). Costs more calls, avoids long-range failure.
  • Multi-step agents: let the model search, read a piece, note findings in a scratchpad, then continue. Anthropic and others describe this as keeping working memory small and external (verify exact terminology).
  • Prompt caching: for a large, stable corpus, cache the prefix to cut cost and latency, but caching does not fix attention quality.
  • Fine-tuning for long context: possible for open-weight models; use synthetic retrieval tasks with positions balanced uniformly. High effort; try prompt and retrieval fixes first.
  • Better models: re-run the position sweep on each new model; the dead zone moves.
  • On-device models: small models on phones (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe LLM Inference) have short effective windows; keep prompts to a few thousand tokens, and use retrieval from a local store. Never push full document sets into a tiny model.

Decision table:

Symptom Likely cause First fix
Answer correct when passage alone, wrong inside 30 chunks lost in the middle plus distractors rerank, cut top_k, edge reorder
Quality falls steadily as chat grows context rot summarise old turns, pin instructions
Model ignores a rule in a long system prompt rule buried mid-prompt move to start and restate at end
Fine on 8k, bad at 150k effective context limit map-reduce or retrieval
Citations point at the wrong document no ids or structure tag documents with ids, ask for quotes

Production incident pattern: a support bot's accuracy dropped two weeks after launch. Nothing in the model changed. Investigation: a new feature appended the customer's full ticket history, pushing the policy document from the top 8 percent of the prompt to the middle 40 percent. Fix: policy first and last-line reminder, ticket history summarised. Lesson: log token counts and the position of key sections, and alert when they shift.

Android angle: a client app should never assemble giant prompts itself. It sends the question to your backend; the backend retrieves, reranks, reorders and calls the model, then returns a short answer and citations. That keeps keys and prompt logic server-side and lets you fix position problems without shipping an app update.

Everyday analogy: if a single huge meeting keeps losing the plot, you do not ask people to listen harder; you split it into smaller meetings with written notes.

Common interview traps.

  • Reaching for a bigger window or fine-tuning before fixing retrieval and ordering.
  • Treating prompt caching as a quality feature. It is cost and latency.
  • Not logging prompt composition, so a regression like the one above is invisible.
  • Proposing to run RAG on-device "to save the server" without noting the small model's tiny effective window.

notes.title: Interview synthesis: joining both topics
notes.html:
Interviewers like to connect the two halves of this note. The connecting thread is that bigger is not automatically better: a bigger model is better only if trained on enough data, and a bigger window is better only if the model can use it.

A short model answer to "Why did labs shift from giant models to smaller, longer-trained ones, and does a longer window make RAG obsolete?":

  • Chinchilla showed that earlier models were undertrained; the optimum balances parameters and tokens at about 20 tokens per parameter for training cost alone (L = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta, C = 6ND).
  • Because inference is paid on every request, teams overtrain smaller models (8B on 15T tokens, about 1,900 tokens per parameter) to get a cheaper model of similar quality.
  • Long windows let you pass more text, but accuracy depends on position and length: primacy and recency win, the middle is weak, and softmax dilution makes each token's share of attention fall as 1/n.
  • So the architecture is: retrieve and rerank to a few chunks, place the best at the edges, ask for quotes, measure with a position sweep, and use long context for tasks that truly need cross-document reasoning.

Numbers to have ready:

  • 6ND FLOPs; N = sqrt(C/120) at 20 tokens per parameter.
  • 70B on 1.4T tokens reproduces the Chinchilla budget of about 5.9e23 FLOPs.
  • Same-compute loss gap between overtrained 8B and optimal 77B is about 0.02 nats, but the 77B costs about 9.6 times more per generated token.
  • Softmax dilution example: weight 0.129 at n = 1,000 versus 0.0015 at n = 100,000.

Questions an interviewer may ask next, with one-line answers:

  • "How would you test if your model suffers from it?" Position sweep at several lengths with real distractors.
  • "What would you change first?" Fewer, reranked chunks; best at the edges; question last.
  • "How do you know when to retrain versus prompt-engineer?" If a sweep shows a position gap with the gold passage alone being answered correctly, try retrieval and ordering first; only fine-tune an open-weight model when those fail and you control the data.
  • "Does MoE change Chinchilla?" Yes, use active parameters for compute and expect different constants (see 04_T2).

Everyday analogy: a big warehouse (window) helps only if the staff can find things in it, and a huge factory (model) helps only if it gets enough raw material (data). Capacity without use is waste.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering the two topics as unrelated facts instead of one story about using capacity well.
  • Giving numbers without a derivation. Always show 6ND or the softmax arithmetic.
  • Declaring a trend final. Scaling regimes and long-context quality are fast-moving; say "as of the latest results I know, verify".
  • Citing Chinchilla constants or exact lost-in-the-middle accuracies from memory with false precision.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Scaling laws. Loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute. The Chinchilla form is L = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta with fitted constants near E = 1.69, alpha = 0.34, beta = 0.28 (verify). Training compute is C = 6ND (2 forward plus 4 backward FLOPs per parameter per token). For minimum training cost use about 20 tokens per parameter, N = sqrt(C/120).

Beyond Chinchilla. Serving costs about 2N per generated token, so for heavily used models a smaller model trained on far more tokens wins on lifetime cost. Example: 8B on 15T tokens loses only about 0.02 nats to a 77B at equal training compute while being about 9.6 times cheaper per token. Limits: diminishing D^-beta returns and the data wall.

Using the laws. Fit on tuned small runs across several orders of magnitude, subtract the floor, give error bars, and verify on a held-back mid-size run. Loss is not capability; data quality, post-training, architecture and test-time compute shift the picture.

Lost in the middle. Accuracy over position is U shaped: primacy and recency are strong, the middle is weak (Liu et al., 2023). Contributing causes: causal masking and attention sinks, positional decay (RoPE), softmax dilution, thin long-range training data, and look-alike distractors. Newer models are better but not immune on multi-fact tasks.

Fixes. Measure with a position sweep on your own data. Rerank and trim chunks, put the best at the edges, question last, quote then answer, tag documents with ids, compress history, restate key rules at the end. Escalate to retrieval pipelines, map-reduce or agents with scratchpads when needed. Log prompt composition so regressions are visible.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Balance parameters and tokens, about 20 per parameter, for training cost; overtrain smaller models for serving cost."
  • "C = 6ND: two FLOPs forward, four backward."
  • "A bigger window is capacity, not comprehension; measure the effective context on your own task."
  • "Put the best evidence at the edges, the question last, and fewer chunks in between."
